flashcards.q: Why doesn't reference counting alone collect a reference cycle (a.ref=b, b.ref=a)?
flashcards.a: Each object's refcount includes a reference from within the cycle itself, so it never reaches zero even after nothing outside the cycle refers to either object. The cyclic GC exists specifically to find and break these cycles via a periodic mark-and-sweep-style scan.

flashcards.q: What is the generational hypothesis and why does it justify scanning gen0 more often than gen2?
flashcards.a: Most objects are short-lived; a much smaller fraction survive to become long-lived. Scanning long-lived objects on every pass would waste effort re-checking objects statistically unlikely to have newly become garbage -- promoting survivors to less-frequently-scanned generations concentrates GC effort where garbage is actually likely to be found.

flashcards.q: What changed in Python 3.4 (PEP 442) regarding __del__ and cycles?
flashcards.a: Pre-3.4, cycles containing objects with __del__ methods couldn't be safely collected at all (no safe finalization order), leaking permanently. PEP 442 introduced a safer finalization protocol allowing such cycles to be collected. __del__ timing is still non-deterministic though -- use context managers for deterministic cleanup.

flashcards.q: Leak vs fragmentation -- what's the diagnostic tell that distinguishes them?
flashcards.a: Leak: tracemalloc/memray show growing Python-level allocations directly (objects genuinely still referenced). Fragmentation: tracemalloc/memray show stable, small allocations, but process RSS won't drop -- that MISMATCH itself is the signal pointing at fragmentation, not a leak.

flashcards.q: Why can pymalloc leave RSS elevated even after all Python objects are correctly freed?
flashcards.a: pymalloc groups memory into ~1MB arenas; an arena can only be returned to the OS once EVERY object within it is freed. Even one surviving small object in an otherwise-empty arena keeps the whole arena claimed, invisible to the OS as free memory.

flashcards.q: tracemalloc vs memray -- overhead and visibility differences?
flashcards.a: tracemalloc: stdlib, Python-level only, ~20-30% overhead, full call stack per allocation -- good for bounded debugging. memray: <5% overhead, sees C-extension/native allocations tracemalloc structurally cannot, attaches to a LIVE process without restart -- the practical production-incident default.

flashcards.q: What is the standard tracemalloc leak-hunting workflow?
flashcards.a: Take a snapshot, run the suspect code path, take a second snapshot, use compare_to() to get a ranked diff by allocation site (file:line) -- isolates the actual leak location far faster than manual code review.

flashcards.q: Why can a closure unintentionally keep a large object alive far longer than expected?
flashcards.a: Closures capture by reference to the enclosing scope, not by value -- referencing even one attribute of a large object keeps the WHOLE object alive as long as the closure is reachable. Fix: extract just the needed value into a local variable before defining the closure.

flashcards.q: Why can a stored exception traceback cause unexpectedly large memory retention?
flashcards.a: A traceback holds a reference to every stack frame between where the exception was raised and caught, and each frame holds all its local variables -- storing a traceback long-lived (e.g. in a logging structure) keeps every one of those locals alive for as long as the traceback is referenced.

flashcards.q: When is gc.disable() defensible vs risky?
flashcards.a: Defensible for short-lived worker processes that exit before enough cycles accumulate to matter (natural process teardown reclaims everything anyway). Risky as a default for long-running services -- any cycles formed while disabled accumulate indefinitely, turning transient garbage into an unbounded leak for the service's whole uptime.
